description: We're using NISAR radar to show how the ground shifts at mine sites in the United States, as a clear, interactive time-lapse anyone can follow.
summary:
How can we identify ground movement across large areas where instruments cannot monitor every location?

GoldRadar InSAR — GroundMotion is an interactive research demonstration that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations into maps of relative surface deformation.

Using quality screening, displacement time-series analysis, and comparisons across satellite viewing tracks, the system highlights areas that warrant closer investigation. A public dashboard lets visitors explore the results and their limitations.

Our current demonstration covers three Nevada mining-area study cells and reports six screened movement features. At Cortez District, one feature has a peak modeled vertical displacement of −170.2 mm and a mean of −134.7 mm across the analyzed observation window (26 June–19 September 2026).

The approach could help researchers investigate changes around communities, roads, and industrial land where suitable data exist. These are preliminary, satellite-derived estimates—not independently ground-validated measurements or predictions of structural failure.
details:
GoldRadar InSAR — GroundMotion

The Problem:

Ground Movement Is Difficult to Observe Everywhere

The ground beneath our communities, roads, industrial facilities and other infrastructure is not always stationary. Natural processes and human activities can cause gradual sinking, uplift or uneven surface movement.

Ground-based instruments can measure these changes precisely, but instruments cannot practically be installed at every location across large landscapes.

We need ways to observe broader patterns of ground movement and identify where closer investigation may be useful.

Our Solution

GoldRadar InSAR introduces GroundMotion, an interactive research application that uses observations from the NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to investigate changes in Earth's surface.

By processing repeat satellite radar observations, GroundMotion produces relative displacement estimates and displays them on a geographic dashboard.

Users can explore monitored areas, examine movement patterns, review satellite observation histories and understand the quality limitations of the measurements.

How It Works

GroundMotion follows five scientific processing stages:

  1. Collect satellite observations: Retrieve NISAR radar products for selected geographic areas.
  2. Filter unreliable measurements: Use radar coherence and phase corrections to reduce noise and unsuitable observations.
  3. Estimate surface movement: Analyze observations collected over time to estimate relative displacement.
  4. Compare satellite viewing directions: Examine measurements from different radar tracks to identify more consistent movement patterns.
  5. Visualize the results: Present screened features, displacement measurements and supporting information through an interactive map.

Where sufficient observation geometry exists, the research workflow estimates vertical and east–west displacement components.

The system's quality categories reflect internal screening criteria, not independently verified measurement accuracy.

Our Research Results

We examined three mining-area study cells in Nevada, United States:

  • Cortez District: Two screened movement features, with a maximum modeled vertical displacement of −170.2 mm.
  • Round Mountain: One screened feature, with a peak modeled vertical displacement of −142.2 mm.
  • Carlin Trend: Three screened features, with the largest modeled vertical displacement reaching −87.1 mm.

The observation window extends from 26 June to 19 September 2026.

At Cortez, the largest feature has a peak modeled vertical displacement of −170.2 mm and a mean of −134.7 mm. These are different statistics for the same feature.

In total, the demonstration reports six screened movement features across three Nevada study areas.

These results are preliminary satellite-derived estimates. Independent GNSS, levelling and other external validation remain necessary.

Innovation and Potential Impact

GroundMotion combines satellite radar processing, time-series analysis, multi-track screening and interactive visualization in a research application.

Its value is not limited to mining.

With suitable satellite observations and further validation, similar methods could support research into ground movement around residential areas, roads, industrial sites, agricultural landscapes and other environments.

The long-term goal is to make scientific ground-deformation information easier to understand and more useful for planning further investigations.

Technology and NASA Data

The research uses NISAR GUNW interferometric observations and supporting GCOV radar products distributed through NASA Earthdata and the Alaska Satellite Facility.

The application uses Python-based scientific processing and web technologies including PHP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

GroundMotion builds upon OREX's existing GoldRadar InSAR research infrastructure.

The public geographic interface uses third-party mapping resources, which are acknowledged in the project references.

Limitations and Future Research

The current results have not been independently ground-validated. Relative surface displacement does not automatically indicate structural damage or imminent failure.

Future development will focus on independent validation, additional observation periods, uncertainty assessment and testing across different landscapes.

GroundMotion is a scientific research and screening tool, not an operational structural-safety warning system.
